title: Enhanced analogue quantum computation with a logically-encoded XX gadget
authors: Robert J. Banks, Natasha Feinstein, Roopayan Ghosh, Sebastian Schulz, Kristel Michielsen, Sougato Bose, P. A. Warburton
abstract: The introduction of two-body XX interactions has been shown to improve the performance of quantum annealing in solving certain combinatorial optimisation problems and would enable the simulation of a broader class of many-body Hamiltonians. Due to experimental constraints, such interactions are typically not natively available on analogue quantum devices. To overcome this limitation we introduce the truss gadget. This is an exact construction that generates two-body XX interactions using only one-body X and Z fields and two-body ZZ interactions which are readily accessible on, for instance, superconducting quantum annealers. We experimentally validate the construction by reproducing the dynamics of a target XX Hamiltonian on a trapped-ion quantum processor. We then apply the gadget to an illustrative set of instances of the weighted maximum-independent-set problem on a superconducting quantum annealer. We empirically determine an approximate thousand-fold improvement in the probability of finding a state close to the ground state for these instances, over implementation without an XX interaction.
summary: This paper introduces the 'truss gadget,' an exact physical circuit design that generates necessary two-body XX interactions using only readily available one-body X/Z fields and ZZ interactions. By experimentally validating this gadget on trapped ions and applying it to the maximum-independent-set problem, the authors demonstrate a significant, thousand-fold enhancement in ground state finding probability compared to implementations lacking the XX coupling.
main_problem: The primary challenge is overcoming hardware limitations in analogue quantum computation that prevent the native implementation of beneficial two-body XX interactions required for simulating complex Hamiltonians.
main_result: The proposed 'truss gadget' provides an exact, hardware-compatible construction to generate effective XX interactions, leading to an approximate thousand-fold improvement in finding the ground state for the weighted maximum-independent-set problem.
method: The authors introduce the truss gadget, a specific physical circuit construction, and validate its dynamics both through theoretical derivation and experimental measurement on a trapped-ion quantum processor.
model_or_system: The system involves quantum annealing/adiabatic quantum computation, where the logical qubits are encoded using physical qubits via the truss gadget. The physical realization utilizes accessible one-body X/Z fields and two-body ZZ interactions.
key_observables: Probability of finding a state close to the ground state for the maximum-independent-set problem; time evolution of occupation probabilities.
important_parameters: The improvement factor of $\sim 10^3$ in ground state probability; the physical Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{	ext{Truss}}^{	ext{Phys}}$ and the resulting logical Hamiltonian $	ilde{H}_{	ext{Truss}}^{	ext{Logical}}$.
main_assumptions: The gadget construction is exact and does not rely on asymptotically large energy penalties, although the comparison to other gadget types highlights inherent trade-offs.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the truss gadget structure on physical qubits, compare the time evolution of probability distributions between the target XX Hamiltonian and the truss gadget implementation, and show the physical graph structure for the encoded problem.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the need for XX interactions in quantum annealing, to introducing the truss gadget as a superior construction, validating its dynamics experimentally on trapped ions, and finally applying it to solve a specific combinatorial optimization problem (MWIS).
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the crucial engineering bottleneck in quantum computation: mapping desired high-level interactions (like XX) onto the limited native couplings of current hardware (like ZZ and X/Z fields).
